newsitem.title: UK: Japan's borrowers may hurt if MOF taxes foreigners.
newsitem.headline: Japan's borrowers may hurt if MOF taxes foreigners.

text.p: Japan's corporations could be forced out of international bond markets if Tokyo scraps a tax exemption law for foreign bond-holders, a senior bond market participant told Reuters on Friday.

Clifford Dammers, secretary general of the International Primary Market Association (IPMA), said the association wrote a letter to Japan's Ministry of Finance (MOF) urging it not to rescind the tax-exemption law for foreigners.

"If the Japanese corporates are forced out of the markets, it would be bad news because we would lose a very attractive class of issuers," Dammers said. The MOF plans to reintroduce the withholding tax for non-Japanese residents on income gains made from investments in Eurobonds including common Euroyen bonds. The MOF first raised the plan in early October, saying it wanted to repeal the law to close a loophole which domestic investors were exploiting by buying the bonds through the overseas subsidiaries of Japanese firms.
Dammers said the advantage of Japan's corporations being competitive in the internatinal market outweighed the possible loss from tax-evasion.
"The trade-off in the case is that you deny access to the international markets to the Japanese corporations," he said.
Analysts estimated more than 100 Japanese corporations and banks have tapped the international capital market since the beginning of 1995 raising several trillion yen.
"If you have a problem with people not paying tax, tackle it at the root of the problem -- the tax-payer and the investor," Dammers said.
He cited examples across Britain, Germany, the United States and Australia where withholding taxes were scrapped.
If the ban on the law goes ahead, Japanese borrowers would have to pay a higher rate of interest to entice investors who may have more attractive alternatives elsewhere, he said.
"It would be bad news for the Japanese because they would be forced back to their domestic markets," Dammers said.
The increased domestic demand would exert upward pressure on interest rates and crowd out small- to medium-size companies, he said.
"If the interest rate is pushed up and there is the crowding-out effect, it's not Sony that's getting particularly hurt. It's the small guy," he said.
Dammers urged Japan to consider using better tax-collection methods, for example not allowing investors to hold bearer bonds as is the case in the United States.

He warned against an alternative proposal to the MOF that required bond holders to produce identification when dealing in bonds because the bureaucracy involved would ground the secondary markets to a halt.
Other institutions on Friday also urged the MOF to uphold the tax-exemption law for foreigners.
Three major Swiss banks, Credit Suisse, Swiss Bank Corp and UBS, jointly submitted a petition to the MOF, urging it to reconsider its plan, bank officials said.
The petition stated the repeal of the tax exemption law could also affect Switzerland's capital market of Switzerland.
